prompt: RSA rests on a gap: multiplying two large primes is easy, while factoring their product is hard. Suppose someone publishes a fast factoring algorithm. Work out which part of the scheme collapses.
answer: The private key, which is recoverable from the public modulus
choices: Key generation, which relies on producing two large primes quickly
The private key, which is recoverable from the public modulus
Encryption, which could no longer scramble the message
Nothing, since the modulus was public from the start
explain: Factoring the public modulus n recovers the secret primes p and q, hence (p - 1)(q - 1) and the private exponent. Generating keys and encrypting messages would still work exactly as before; what is lost is the secrecy of the private key, which is the whole of the security.
